seasons.review_body: The debut season of Philipp Kassbohrer and Matthias Murmann's German black comedy arrived on Netflix in May 2019 and distinguished itself immediately from the crowded teen-crime genre by grounding its premise in fact - the real Leipzig ecstasy operation of 2015. Moritz Zimmermann, desperate to win back his girlfriend who returned from an American exchange with upgraded confidence and cooler friends, partners with hacker Lenny to sell MDMA through the darknet. The first six episodes play the escalation for both laughs and dread, and the trick works: an 89% Rotten Tomatoes aggregate across the series reflects critics who appreciated how the show keeps the comedy alive even as the stakes become genuinely criminal. The bildundtonfabrik production understood that the funniest version of this premise is also the most accurate - the operation is run by people who have no business running an operation.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# How To Sell Drugs Online Fast S1E1: "StartUp" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The first instruction fits on a warning label: if you sell large quantities online, do not “tell total strangers about it.” The episode then builds a boy who cannot stop telling the wrong person the wrong thing at the wrong time. **Moritz** wants a welcome-home present, a repaired relationship, and a plan that makes **Daniel Riffert** arrive empty-handed. He gets login fights, party politics, a cloud threat, and an anonymous call that points enforcement toward a Capoeira address. BollyAI's read: “StartUp” works because its hero treats control like software, while the episode keeps proving the system has users.

## Control Is the First Bad Idea

The pilot’s sharpest move is making Moritz’s emotional problem look technical. His conflict with **Lisa** begins with access: her account, her decision, her definition of “taking a break.” their argument over him logging into her account marks him as needy and gives the episode its operating principle. Moritz keeps mistaking proximity for permission.

That matters because the relationship language is slippery by design. “Taking a break” becomes a public status at the party, soft enough to avoid a clean breakup and cruel enough to let both sides read it differently. Moritz wants to win Lisa back by managing the environment around her. If Daniel arrives with drugs, Moritz loses ground. If Daniel is blocked, Moritz imagines a lane opening.

The writing is strongest when it keeps the mistake ordinary. Moritz does not begin as a spotlighted kingpin. He begins as a teenager trying to solve jealousy with logistics. That is funnier, smaller, and more dangerous. The online-drug warning in the first minute gives the hour a crime frame, but the engine is wounded teen control. The gap between those scales is the joke. A personal insecurity is already learning to speak in operational language.

## MyTems Gives the Scam a Clean Shirt

The project pitch is the episode’s neatest camouflage. MyTems sounds tidy: a place for trading game items online instead of using shady Darknet forums. The pitch places Moritz and his circle in a world where marketplaces, accounts, and digital trust are normal teenage tools. The show does not have to drag him into a criminal universe. It only has to slide the purpose of an existing system sideways.

The account-money beat sharpens that slide. Moritz wants to keep the situation contained, yet he uses their project money and triggers consequences when **Ute** confronts him about where the gift money came from. That is the central contradiction in miniature: he reaches for a clean fix and contaminates the one practical structure he has.

The episode earns its title here. “StartUp” sounds like a cute label for young people around a digital project, but it plays as a diagnosis. Moritz already has the founder disease: he believes the product, the pitch, and the workaround can outrun the human mess underneath. The hour is smart enough to show the boring infrastructure before the chaos. Money, accounts, routines, addresses. Crime in this pilot is less a leap than a rebrand.

## The Party Turns Romance Into Logistics

Lisa’s welcome-back party gives the episode its cleanest social trap. She wants control over who gets included, and she tells Dan the pills are the ticket to get in. That single condition changes the party from a teen gathering into a delivery problem. Desire gets routed through supply.

The MDMA lecture fits that structure. The episode identifies the drug, its effects, its timing, and the next-morning downside. On paper, that could have played like a blunt explainer. Here, it works because it arrives before the party logistics tighten. The information turns ecstasy from vague contraband into a scheduled object. It has onset, consequences, and social value. It can make someone wanted at the door.

Moritz’s plan against Daniel grows out of that arithmetic. If Daniel brings the pills, he has value. If Moritz prevents that, Daniel loses his ticket. The romantic triangle is being processed like a marketplace problem, and the episode keeps finding comedy in how ugly that processing becomes.

The weakness is visible in this stretch. The hour jumps hard: online-drug framing, relationship fight, project pitch, drug lesson, party access, threat, tip. The rapid exchange gives the pilot speed, but it leaves some emotional beats gasping. Lisa and Moritz’s “break” has bite, yet the episode sprints toward mechanics before the hurt can settle. The pace is a weapon. Once or twice, it cuts past the bruise.

## The Cloud Threat Makes Secrecy Feel Outdated the episode lands its most modern little punchline: a threat about a photo being sent to Facebook contacts is undercut because it is already on the cloud. The beat is small, but it nails the show’s environment. Privacy is not a door with a lock. It is backups, accounts, contacts, and leverage.

That matters for Moritz because containment is his fantasy. He wants Daniel intercepted. He wants Lisa’s party controlled. He wants the project money bent toward his personal mission and then explained away. The cloud-photo beat says the world he lives in does not reward that fantasy. Information has copies. Plans have notifications. Evidence travels without asking.

This is where the pilot’s form matches its subject. The abrupt topic switches in the dossier are not accidental texture. They make the episode feel like a browser with too many tabs open, each one capable of ruining the other. The personal plot and the criminal plot keep interrupting each other because, for Moritz, they are already the same plot.

The strongest comedy in “StartUp” comes from that collapse. Nobody needs to deliver a grand speech about digital life. A photo, an account, a party invite, and a marketplace pitch do the work. The episode trusts interfaces and petty motives to expose character. That trust gives the pilot its snap.

## The Anonymous Tip Opens the Bigger Machine

The call changes the scale. “I have some interesting information for you,” the caller says, before naming Daniel Riffert as someone selling ecstasy at the school and giving a specific Capoeira address. The line is simple, almost procedural. Its plainness works. Moritz’s scheme has moved from teenage maneuvering into a world where names, addresses, and enforcement can enter the chat.

The episode plants useful open loops without overdecorating them. Will Moritz’s Plan B and the cloud-photo threat expose the group’s drug scheme? Will Daniel still reach Lisa’s party with ecstasy? Will the anonymous tip lead to arrests at the named address? Each question grows from a concrete action already on screen, which keeps the cliffhanger from feeling pasted on.

The ending also gives the pilot its best argument about Moritz. He thinks he is arranging pieces on a board. By the final stretch, he has become one of the pieces. Using project money has pulled Ute into the consequences. Targeting Daniel has pointed outside attention toward a named place. Trying to win Lisa back has made the whole ecosystem louder.

That is the promising engine for the season. The pilot does not need Moritz to be powerful yet. It only needs him to be clever enough to cause damage and insecure enough to keep going.

## The Verdict

“StartUp” is a strong pilot with one clean thesis: Moritz wants to control the mess, and every tool he uses makes the mess easier to trace. The episode’s best craft lies in how naturally it connects teen jealousy to digital systems. Accounts, cloud storage, project money, online trading, and a named address all become pressure points. The hour is fast, funny in its specifics, and built around consequences instead of empty swagger.

The downside is compression. A few emotional turns, especially around Moritz and Lisa’s break, would hit harder with more room between plot beats. Still, the pace mostly works because the episode’s world is supposed to feel overconnected. As a season opener, it plants a sturdy engine: one boy’s private plan is already becoming a public problem.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp pilot where Moritz treats heartbreak like a system problem and immediately starts breaking the system.

bollymeter.basis: Critic consensus held at the same 89% aggregate; the season escalated the operation's scale while maintaining the black-comedy balance that made the first series work.

seasons.review_body: Season 2, released July 2020, pushed MyDrugs.de from bedroom startup into something that required genuine criminal infrastructure. The show added new characters to reflect the expanding operation's need for logistics, security and money-laundering, and the writing maintained the central irony that made season 1 work: these are teenagers who are very good at something they should not be doing at all. The coming-of-age framework continued to carry weight - Moritz's motivations shifted from romantic desperation to something closer to identity, and Lenny's arc deepened. Critics maintained the overall 89% aggregate approval. The season is most effective when it remembers that the comedy of incompetence only works if the audience believes in the competence that keeps enabling it.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 trades the shock of the premise for the more difficult comedy of scale - running a drug empire is, it turns out, boring in ways that are very funny.

bollymeter.basis: Third season maintained the 89% average Tomatometer; concluded the original story arc that the series had been building since the Leipzig-inspired premise of season 1.

seasons.review_body: The third season, arriving July 2021, brought the original character arcs toward resolution while raising the legal and criminal stakes to a level that tested the show's commitment to its comedy registers. Moritz and Lenny now operated in a world where the consequences of their decisions were no longer theoretical, and the best episodes balanced that weight against the absurdity that had characterised the series from the start. The show remained rooted in its German specificity - the Leipzig geography, the particular social dynamics of the characters' school world - even as the plot expanded outward. Critics held the 89% aggregate, suggesting the show maintained its quality even if the novelty of the premise had naturally diminished by year three.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 closes the loop on the original operation with consequences that the first season's comic register could not quite have anticipated.

seasons.review_body: Season 4, released April 2025, arrived after a nearly four-year gap and served as the series finale. Reception data was not yet aggregated at time of authoring. The season marks the formal conclusion to the story begun by the real-life Leipzig events of 2015, and its critical standing will depend on whether the show found a way to close the premise with the same dark wit that opened it.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 returns after a long gap and faces the challenge of making a finale feel earned for characters who were, by design, always running faster than they should.
